clinicalPearls: Distinguished from type 2 by dystopia canthorum, the lateral displacement of the inner canthi with normally positioned pupils and outer canthi.
Caused by heterozygous PAX3 variants and inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with variable expressivity.
Pigmentary features include a white forelock, premature greying, patchy skin hypopigmentation and heterochromia or brilliant blue irides.
Congenital sensorineural hearing loss occurs but is less frequent than in type 2, reflecting the diagnostic effect of the W index.
A broad high nasal root, medial eyebrow flare and synophrys are characteristic facial signs.
Dystopia canthorum can make the palpebral fissures appear narrow and the interpupillary distance normal despite an increased inner-canthal distance.
The W index, combining canthal and pupillary measurements, is used to confirm dystopia canthorum objectively.
As a neurocristopathy, features arise from deficient melanocyte development; hearing and pigment problems should prompt audiological and ophthalmological review.
reference.pathophysiology: Waardenburg syndrome type 1 is an autosomal dominant neurocristopathy caused by heterozygous loss-of-function variants in PAX3, a paired-box transcription factor essential for the specification, survival and migration of neural crest-derived melanocytes. Melanocytes populate the skin, hair, iris stroma and, critically, the stria vascularis of the cochlea, where they are required for normal endolymphatic homoeostasis and hair-cell function. Haploinsufficiency of PAX3 leads to regional absence or reduction of melanocytes, producing the pigmentary features (white forelock, heterochromia, skin patches) and, when the cochlea is affected, congenital sensorineural hearing loss. PAX3 also influences the development of periocular mesenchyme, and its disruption is associated with dystopia canthorum, the lateral displacement of the inner canthi that clinically separates type 1 from type 2. The disorder shows marked variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance for individual features, so relatives sharing the same variant may display very different combinations of pigmentary, facial and auditory signs.
additionalDifferentials: Waardenburg syndrome type 2 (no dystopia canthorum, more frequent deafness)
Waardenburg syndrome type 3 (PAX3-related with additional limb/musculoskeletal anomalies)
Piebaldism (KIT-related patchy depigmentation without dystopia canthorum or deafness)
Vitiligo and other acquired depigmenting disorders
Isolated heterochromia iridis of benign or other cause
Tietz syndrome and other MITF-spectrum pigmentary-auditory conditions
additionalInvestigations: Audiological assessment including newborn hearing screening and pure-tone audiometry
Ophthalmological examination documenting iris colour, heterochromia and canthal position
Objective canthal and pupillary measurement to calculate the W index for dystopia canthorum
Molecular genetic testing of PAX3 to confirm the diagnosis
Dermatological review of hypopigmented patches and hair depigmentation
Family assessment and pedigree analysis given autosomal dominant inheritance
Developmental and speech evaluation where hearing loss is present
redFlags: Confirmed congenital sensorineural hearing loss requiring early intervention
Bilateral profound deafness affecting language acquisition
New neurological or bowel symptoms suggesting an alternative Waardenburg subtype
Family history of deafness with pigmentary features indicating at-risk relatives
Progressive visual or ocular concerns beyond stable heterochromia
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy is normal and the pigmentary and facial features are non-progressive; the main functional impact is congenital sensorineural hearing loss, which when present is stable and well managed with amplification or cochlear implantation. Prognosis is dominated by auditory rehabilitation outcomes.
pitfalls: Missing dystopia canthorum and misclassifying the case as type 2
Relying on interpupillary distance alone, which is normal, and overlooking the increased inner-canthal distance
Assuming absent hearing loss excludes the diagnosis given variable penetrance
Attributing the white forelock or heterochromia to unrelated causes
Failing to examine and counsel relatives who may carry the variant with subtle signs
